title: Emergent Learning in Action: The After Action Review
author: Charles Parry
summary: Charles Parry describes the U.S. Army's After Action Review (AAR) as a model of emergent learning, in which knowledge is discovered and used inside ongoing work rather than transmitted by outside experts. He traces how early critique-style reviews at the National Training Center put units on the defensive, and how the Army shifted the observer role to expert facilitator and pushed reviews down to the platoon level. Parry then shows how Harley-Davidson, Geerlings & Wade and Power Construction adapted the practice for business. He argues the AAR is a continuing practice, not a one-off meeting or post-mortem, and identifies four patterns behind successful use: localness, forward focus, punctuation and iteration. He closes with two pitfalls to avoid and concrete next steps for leaders who want to start.
points: The AAR rests on three questions: what was supposed to happen, what actually happened and why, and what the team will do the same or differently next time.
The Army learned that expert-led critique and checklists put leaders on the defensive, so the observer became a facilitator who helps the team discover its own lessons.
Unlike a post-mortem, an AAR is a forward-focused practice that feeds lessons into the next similar event, so it needs iteration over at least four or five sessions to build trust.
Four patterns (localness, forward focus, punctuation and iteration) help leaders choose a repeating work event and make the learning stick.
Teams should run the AAR first for their own benefit, not to build a knowledge base for outsiders, or the practice will not be sustained.
quotes: One of the best sources of actionable knowledge is that which emerges from people’s own experience
Unlike post-mortems, the AAR is a continuing practice that is focused forward, generating lessons to be applied in the immediate future by the same people who developed them.
In a complex modern battlefield, the Army needed broadly skilled, thinking soldiers, not technicians with their faces in the rulebook.
We’re not opening 16 warehouses. We’re opening one warehouse 16 times.
The Army thinks learning has not occurred until an insight shapes actual behavior and is validated by results.
The first and best customers of a learning practice must be those directly involved.
In a complex and dynamic world, every action plan, every strategic plan, every leader’s initiative is in fact a working hypothesis
